name: Marsanne

lines.s10: Marsanne is the broad, waxy white of Hermitage in the northern Rhône, quiet in scent, with ripe pear, almond and honeysuckle.
lines.s20: Marsanne is the main white grape of the northern Rhône, around the hill of Hermitage. It is dry, full and waxy, with ripe pear, almond and honeysuckle, and with years in bottle it turns to honey and toasted hazelnut.
lines.s45: Marsanne does the quiet work in the white wines of the northern Rhône, at Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray. It is not a perfumed grape. It gives ripe pear, white peach and almond, with a waxy feel, a full body and soft acidity. With years in bottle it deepens to honey and toasted hazelnut. The Rhône often ferments it in barrel with a little Roussanne, while Victoria in Australia tends to make it alone, in steel, with no oak at all. Pour it with veal in cream, roast pork or crab. Some of Victoria's vines, planted in 1927, still give a crop each year.
lines.sale: Marsanne is the broad shouldered white of the Rhône: ripe pear, almond and a waxy, mouth filling feel, with no loud perfume. I would pour it with the roast pork or the veal, where a lighter white would disappear.

glass.lead: Ripe pear, white peach and almond with honeysuckle and beeswax, on a full, waxy body with soft acidity.

ladder.where: Cassis in Provence, California's Central Coast, Victoria's Goulburn Valley

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low to medium, alcohol medium to high, body full, with an oily, waxy texture.

old.where: Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray; Cassis; the Valais
old.glass: Tends to be broad and waxy: ripe pear, white peach, honeysuckle and almond, with soft acidity and a faint bitter grip. It often closes for some years, then opens to honey and toasted hazelnut.
old.cellar: Usually blended with a little Roussanne and fermented in barrel or large cask, some of it new; Saint-Péray also makes it sparkling, in the bottle.

new.where: Victoria's Goulburn Valley and Nagambie Lakes; California's Central Coast
new.glass: Victorian wines are typically lighter and unoaked: lemon, honeysuckle and pear when young, delicate and fresh, turning to honey, toast and orange marmalade with bottle age. California tends to be riper, with melon.
new.cellar: In Victoria usually bottled alone under its own name, fermented in steel and released young; California often blends it with Roussanne and Viognier in older barrels.

contrast.why: The Rhône's appellations name a place, and its growers blend the wine and raise it in wood. Victoria has grown Marsanne since the nineteenth century and built its own habit: one grape, steel, and bottle age in place of oak.
contrast.blur: Some Rhône cellars now work in steel for a fresher, earlier wine, and oaked Australian bottlings and California blends can come close to a white Saint-Joseph.
contrast.call: Waxy weight, almond and a touch of vanilla from barrel lean Rhône; lemon and honeysuckle at lighter weight, or toast with no oak, lean Victoria.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; a young unoaked wine a little cooler.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wide Burgundy bowl for a mature Hermitage.
service.decant: Rarely needed. A mature white Hermitage can open with a gentle decant; taste a sample first.
service.age: It often closes after its first few years and opens again after five; white Hermitage keeps for decades.

with.dish: Roast pork or veal in cream
with.why: a full, waxy white meets the richness
weight and soft acidity suit sweet shellfish
almond and honey in the wine echo the roast

with.dish: Redfish with almonds and brown butter
with.why: the wine's almond note meets the browned butter

with.dish: Comté or another hard mountain cheese
with.why: a nutty wine beside a nutty cheese

labels.means: White wine from the hill of Hermitage: mostly Marsanne, often with some Roussanne.
A northern Rhône appellation for Marsanne and Roussanne alone, made still or sparkling.
The name Marsanne takes in the Valais in Switzerland, where it is rich and often sweet.
The classic pair: Marsanne for weight and wax, Roussanne for perfume and acidity.

guest.q: What is in a white Hermitage?
guest.a: Mostly Marsanne, often with some Roussanne. Marsanne gives the weight and the waxy texture, and Roussanne adds perfume and freshness.

guest.q: This older bottle tastes of honey and nuts. Has it gone off?
guest.a: No, that is the grape growing up. Marsanne starts quiet, with pear and almond, and with years in bottle it turns to honey, toasted hazelnut and marmalade while staying dry.
In weight, yes. It is as full, but softer in acidity and waxier, and it tastes of pear and almond where an oaked Chardonnay tastes of butter and toast.

compare.tell: Roussanne is the more aromatic partner, with chamomile tea, pear and fresher acidity; Marsanne is broader, waxier and nuttier.
Viognier is loudly perfumed with apricot and honeysuckle and feels headier; Marsanne is quieter, with pear, almond and beeswax.
Chardonnay carries more acidity and shows butter and toast from the cellar; Marsanne is waxier and softer, with almond and honeysuckle.

cards.front: Marsanne: which northern Rhône appellations make white wine from it?
cards.back: Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray, usually with some Roussanne. Saint-Péray makes it still and sparkling.

cards.front: Marsanne blind: the Rhône or Victoria, what tips it?
cards.back: Waxy weight, almond and a touch of vanilla from barrel lean Rhône. Lemon and honeysuckle at lighter weight, or toast and honey with no oak at all, lean Victoria.

cards.front: What does Marsanne give a Rhône white blend, and Roussanne beside it?
cards.back: Marsanne gives weight, a waxy texture and a reliable crop. Roussanne adds perfume, pear and firmer acidity, and is harder to grow.

questions.q: A blind white is eight years old, dry and medium bodied, with lemon, honeysuckle, honey and toast, and no vanilla or barrel note at all. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Unoaked Victorian Marsanne starts with lemon and honeysuckle and gains honey and toast in bottle. White Hermitage would be fuller and waxier, usually with a note from the barrel.

questions.q: A guest asks which grape gives a white Hermitage its weight and its waxy texture. Which is it?
questions.exp: Marsanne gives white Hermitage its weight and waxy texture. Roussanne, its partner, brings perfume and acidity, and Viognier belongs to Condrieu.

questions.q: A Swiss list from the Valais offers a rich white labelled Ermitage. Which grape is in the bottle?
questions.exp: Ermitage is the Valais name for Marsanne. Chasselas there is Fendant, Silvaner is Johannisberg and Pinot Gris is Malvoisie.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it: the northern Rhône against Victoria's unoaked Marsanne, with California beside it.

No Codex record on Marsanne is believed wrong. Inter Rhône describes its aged note as hazelnut where INTRO_GRAPES says almond and marzipan; the entry gives almond young and toasted hazelnut with age, which holds both.

The ladder has two rungs, moderate and warm, as TASTE.clim and the Régionale row allow. The Goulburn Valley is placed warm; its lemon and honeysuckle come from the unoaked cellar more than from the climate, which the worlds section says.
The vines of 1927 in Victoria stand on the Codex's own Australian record and on Wine Australia's pages; the estate that owns them is not named.

Left out for want of a primary source: the tale of a composer ordering a hundred bottles of Saint-Péray (the Codex's Master bank tells it; a search of the regional body's pages did not confirm the figure) and the naming of the grape after the village of Marsanne near Montélimar (reference works say probably).
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
